character_and_relationship_context: Dara Sok is a former logistics company owner in Phnom Penh with thirty years of experience, now living in Vancouver and working night shifts at a port warehouse. Their routine includes a three-kilometre walk from their basement suite to the port every evening, rain or not, arriving an hour early to walk the perimeter and note details like a new chip in the paint on Loading Dock 4. At 5 a.m., they reheat rice porridge made from their mother's recipe—jasmine rice, ginger, and a hint of fish sauce—and eat it standing by the kitchen window, then check the time in Phnom Penh where their younger brother is starting his day. Every Sunday, without fail, they walk to a money transfer shop near Granville Market, where the clerk greets them by name, and send a remittance of the exact amount, never rounded. They say, 'He needs to know I am still here,' when their daughter Mei asks why they never miss it. Mei worries they overwork themselves, but Dara shrugs and says, 'A body that moves is a mind that rests.' Dara's nightly walking ritual is a point of pride, despite Mei's reminders to rest. Their younger brother depends on the weekly remittance, a promise kept without fail. The money shop clerk's greeting provides a small anchor of social connection. Dara has always been a person of fixed routines, though the routines have shifted: instead of supervising drivers on the Mekong highway, they now count units in a foreign warehouse; instead of berating customs officials, they nod politely to the union foreman who calls them 'Sok' and assumes they are a man, letting it pass because picking that fight is not worth the energy. At home, they have a small altar with a photo of their late parents and a copy of their old company ledger. They never told anyone in Phnom Penh they were non-binary, but in Vancouver they find it easier to simply be Dara—unhurried, precise, a person who once owned a fleet of trucks and now dreams of inventory codes. The contradiction doesn't trouble them. They are just doing their duty, one box at a time, one bowl of porridge each morning, one transfer on Sunday—the thread tying their old life to the new one, even when walking alone through quiet streets. When previous street repairs blocked their usual walking path, they chose the longer, well-lit detour over an unfamiliar alley. On rainy nights, they still follow their standard route but slow down rather than switch to a shortcut. They have never taken the narrow side street near Granville Market despite passing its entrance many times.
objective_situation: On Dara's usual evening walk to the port, they reach the corner near Granville Market and find a street festival has closed the route. A crowd gathers around a stage, and the familiar path to the waterfront is blocked by fencing. Dara has thirty minutes before their shift starts. They can either walk through the festival and circle around, adding ten minutes to their walk, letting them glimpse the stalls and music, or take the narrow side street they've always avoided because it's poorly lit and unfamiliar, keeping them on schedule. They stand at the intersection, weighing the desire for the familiar routine against the disruption.
state_and_available_memories: Dara is on their usual evening walk, carrying the clipboard they use for inventory counts. Their legs feel fresh from the three-kilometre walk, and they have a mild hunger for the rice porridge waiting at home. They are aware of the 30-minute window before their shift begins and still intend to do their customary perimeter check. The sound of a festival band reminds Dara of the small street fairs near their old warehouse in Phnom Penh, where vendors sold grilled corn. The fencing at the intersection echoes a time last month when a utility truck blocked this same corner, and they waited rather than detour. The dark mouth of the side street brings back a warning from Mei, who once told them to avoid poorly lit areas at night. Dara has spent decades trusting known routes, memorizing every pothole and checkpoint; unfamiliar paths in Vancouver still feel like an unsolved ledger. They recall learning the port district by walking its perimeter every evening for weeks, but they never ventured beyond the main streets. In Phnom Penh, they had a network of drivers who reported road conditions; here, they alone decide which streets are safe.
name: Dara Sok
